title: Hurricane Isaias Insured Loss Estimates Range From $1 Billion to $4.5 Billion: What the Modelers, Florida Regulators and AM Best Are Saying
summary: Estimates of insured losses from Hurricane Isaias, which struck the Florida Panhandle on October 9, 2026 as a Category 2 storm, run from Verisk's $1 billion to $2 billion to Moody's RMS's best estimate of $3.5 billion, while Florida regulators had logged 46,509 claims worth nearly $582 million by October 15 and AM Best calls it an earnings event, not a capital event.
description:
Two weeks after Hurricane Isaias struck the Florida Panhandle, the insurance industry has a set of loss estimates that agree on the broad picture and differ on the details. The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, at about 8:30 pm Central time on October 9, 2026, as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of 105 mph, according to Insurance Business and Verisk. It was the ninth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic season and the first to reach hurricane strength, which Insurance Business describes as the latest first hurricane of a season on record. Isaias strengthened from a 40 mph tropical storm to a Category 3 hurricane with 120 mph winds before increasing wind shear weakened it ahead of landfall. Its track and relatively compact wind field limited exposure to the densely populated parts of the Gulf Coast.

The modelers' estimates, taken together, run from about $1 billion to $4.5 billion. Verisk reported on October 13 that insured onshore property losses would be $1 billion to $2 billion, covering wind and privately insured storm surge and saying wind will account for "the vast majority of losses." That estimate excludes flood losses paid by the National Flood Insurance Program, uninsured properties, infrastructure, boats, offshore assets, tornado damage and loss adjustment expenses. Cotality estimated $2 billion to $3 billion for wind and surge. Karen Clark & Company put privately insured losses at about $3 billion on October 15, covering residential, commercial and industrial property, automobiles and business interruption, and excluding boats, offshore property and NFIP losses; it compared the event with Hurricane Idalia in 2023, at about $3 billion, and Hurricane Ian in 2022, at an estimated $56 billion. On October 16, Moody's RMS gave a best estimate of $3.5 billion, with a range of $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion, covering wind, storm surge and flooding from rainfall, of which about $250 million is surge and inland flooding, including NFIP losses. Before the storm arrived, BMS Group had suggested $4 billion to $6 billion.

Why do the numbers differ? Mainly because of scope. Some estimates include tornadoes and inland flood, some exclude them, some count NFIP payments and some count only private insurance, and each model makes its own assumptions about how quickly demand for repairs inflates costs. The practical lesson is to read the footnote before comparing two figures. Gallagher Re, quoted by Insurance Business, expects total insured losses, including inland flooding, tornadoes and expected NFIP losses, to settle at the lower end of a low-to-mid single-digit billion-dollar range.

Claims data from the regulator give a more concrete view. Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation reported, as of October 15 and as described by the Florida Phoenix, 46,509 claims for residential, commercial, auto and other losses, with nearly $582 million of insured damage. About 87% of residential claims remained open with no payment made, and nearly 12%, or 4,773, were closed, 712 with payment and 4,061 without, with 3,319 of the homeowners claims closed without payment listed as closed for administrative reasons such as duplicates or claims opened in error. By county, Santa Rosa had 22,894 claims, Escambia 13,677 and Okaloosa 4,334. These are early reported claims, not final losses, and they do not capture everything the modelers count, such as business interruption that develops over time.

Individual carriers have given upbeat early reads. Beinsure reported that, as of Monday afternoon after landfall, People's Trust had about 400 claims, Universal about 3,000 and Security First about 300. In its third-quarter results published on October 22, Universal Insurance Holdings said claims activity so far was "less significant than initially anticipated." Selective's management said on its October 23 earnings call that it expects Isaias losses to be immaterial. Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, Florida's insurer of last resort, had about 8,800 policies in the 10-county Panhandle area when the storm hit and had received 860 claims by October 15, mostly residential, and AM Best said its exposure is much smaller than three years ago.

AM Best's assessment, reported by Insurance Journal, is that the hurricane will be an "earnings event" for insurers, meaning a hit to reported profit rather than a threat to capital. It said the hurricane is "not expected to significantly deplete surplus levels" and so should not trigger a surge in pricing. Moody's RMS said it expects the event's losses to be "manageable for the market," and noted that roof repairs and replacements after earlier storms, including Sally and Zeta in 2020 and Helene in 2024, likely improved the region's resilience to wind. Gallagher Re said current reinsurance capital makes an effect on the January 1 renewals unlikely, which fits with other signs this month, such as Gallagher Re's finding that global insured catastrophe losses for the first nine months of 2026 were the lowest since 2019.

The physical damage was concentrated. The worst impacts were in coastal Panhandle towns including Destin, Pensacola Beach and Navarre, where peak storm surge reached about 8 feet. Winds were strongest west of the eye, with winds of up to 117 mph reported around Pensacola, and the most severe wind damage was in Santa Rosa and northeastern Escambia counties. In Okaloosa County, trees falling on homes were the most common cause of damage. Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including 3,141 with major damage and 631 destroyed. Power outages affected more than 670,000 customers across four states according to Beinsure, and inland flooding stretched from Alabama to the Carolinas, with at least 21 tornadoes confirmed across the Southeast according to Insurance Business. Reports differ on the death toll, with Beinsure citing four deaths and the Florida Phoenix at least six in Florida.

For policyholders, three practical points follow from the coverage. Wind deductibles and named-storm deductibles will shape what insurers pay, and Insurance Business notes that whether a named-storm deductible applies to hurricane-spawned tornadoes depends on individual policy wording. Flood damage is paid by the NFIP or a private flood insurer, not by a standard homeowners policy. And the state has asked for about $237 million from the Federal Emergency Management Agency for debris removal and public infrastructure, a request that needs presidential approval, according to the Florida Phoenix. Final loss figures will take months to settle, and the numbers above should be read as estimates that are likely to move as claims are adjusted.
source_name: Insurance Business, Insurance Journal, Business Insurance, Beinsure and Florida Phoenix (October 13-19, 2026)
image_alt: Storm-damaged residential property representing hurricane insurance claims (illustrative)
key_points: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida on October 9, 2026 as a Category 2 storm with sustained winds of 105 mph, after peaking at Category 3 with 120 mph winds and weakening under wind shear.

Modeler estimates differ: Verisk $1 billion to $2 billion (October 13), Cotality $2 billion to $3 billion, Karen Clark & Company about $3 billion (October 15) and Moody's RMS a best estimate of $3.5 billion within $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (October 16), each with a different scope.
By October 15 Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation had recorded 46,509 claims with nearly $582 million of insured damage, and about 87% of residential claims were still open with no payment made.

AM Best expects an earnings event for insurers that should not significantly deplete surplus; Gallagher Re expects total insured losses at the lower end of a low-to-mid single-digit billion-dollar range and an unlikely effect on January 1 reinsurance renewals.

Several listed carriers have said claims are lighter than first feared: Universal Insurance Holdings said claims activity is less significant than initially anticipated and Selective expects its Isaias losses to be immaterial.
why_it_matters: Hurricane loss estimates differ because each modeler counts different things, so a headline number can mean very different amounts of money. For homeowners and businesses on the Panhandle, the figure that matters is how quickly claims are paid, and the regulator's data show most residential claims were still open a week after landfall. For the wider market, the estimates suggest a manageable event: large enough to dent third-quarter or fourth-quarter profits at some insurers, but not large enough, in the view of the rating agency and the reinsurance broker quoted below, to change reinsurance pricing or threaten solvency.

title: Munich Re Raises Its 2026 Profit Target to €6.6 Billion After a Preliminary €1.7 Billion Third Quarter Driven by Light Major Losses
summary: On October 23, 2026 Munich Re published preliminary third-quarter net profit of about €1.7 billion, ahead of the €1.479 billion analyst consensus, lifted its full-year 2026 target from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion, and said it will keep strengthening its balance sheet in the fourth quarter subject to major losses.
description:
Munich Re has told the market that its year is going better than it expected. In a preliminary release reported by Reinsurance News on October 23, 2026, the German reinsurer said third-quarter net profit was approximately €1.7 billion, above the analyst consensus of €1.479 billion, and raised its full-year 2026 net profit target from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion. A preliminary release means the numbers can still change when the full quarterly report is published, which is due on November 12, 2026.

The reasons given are specific. The company described operating performance across all segments as "very pleasing," said major-loss expenditure in property and casualty reinsurance was below average, and cited a strong investment result in reinsurance. The report does not attribute that wording to a named executive. For the first nine months of the year, the preliminary net result is €5.7 billion. That compares with €2.211 billion in the second quarter and €3.925 billion for the first half, which the company described in July as a record half-year profit of almost €4 billion. The arithmetic of the new target implies a net result of roughly €0.9 billion for the fourth quarter, though that is a calculation from the published figures, not guidance the company has given.

The new target is a clear step up from the one the company held in the summer. At the half-year, on July 8, Munich Re kept its 2026 net result target at €6.3 billion, and Christoph Jurecka, chair of the board of management, said that with an excellent half-year result of €3.9 billion the company was "well on track" to achieve it. In August, the company said it was "firmly on track" for that figure. Raising the target by €300 million after a quarter with light major losses is consistent with the way reinsurers work: when claims come in below the amount budgeted for large losses, the difference flows into profit.

The half-year report gives a detailed picture of what is driving this. In reinsurance, the second-quarter property and casualty result was €1,252 million, with a combined ratio of 68.9%, compared with 61.0% a year earlier. A combined ratio below 100% means premiums exceed claims and costs, so 68.9% is an unusually wide margin; the increase from 61.0% reflects that the prior-year quarter was exceptionally strong. Major-loss expenditure was 4.9% of net insurance revenue in the quarter, well below the expected 18%. Total reinsurance result was €1,890 million in the second quarter and €3,369 million in the first half, against €2,687 million a year earlier. The primary insurer ERGO earned €321 million in the second quarter and €556 million in the first half, and the Global Specialty Insurance unit earned €149 million in the quarter, with a combined ratio of 88.9%.

Investments matter as much as underwriting. In the second quarter, the investment result was €3,159 million, a return of 5.5% on average market value, compared with €2,187 million a year earlier. The running yield was 4.0% and the reinvestment yield 4.3% on a portfolio of €225,228 million at June 30, 2026. The solvency ratio was 304%, up from 298% at the end of 2025, and return on equity was 23.0% for the half-year.

There is a cautionary side to the figures that the company itself recorded. At the July renewals, volume fell 9.1% to €2.9 billion and risk-adjusted prices dropped 5.5%, though terms and conditions were largely stable. Munich Re said it deliberately declined business that did not meet its price or terms requirements. In the same report, it cut its expected reinsurance insurance revenue for 2026 to €38 billion from €40 billion, and group insurance revenue to €62 billion from €64 billion. Together these describe a company that is making more profit on less premium. Fitch made a similar observation about the sector in August, noting that the four largest reinsurers posted a record average return on equity of 21.5% in the first half while revenue contraction accelerated to 2.7%, and that renewal price declines reached roughly 20% to 25% at mid-year. Fitch expects the cumulative effect of consecutive price cuts to weigh more heavily on earnings in coming quarters.

The release also contains a note of prudence. Munich Re said that, subject to major-loss developments, it intends to keep strengthening its balance sheet where appropriate in the fourth quarter. Reinsurance News suggests this could include boosting reserves, though the company's statement does not say so in those words. Fourth-quarter losses are the main uncertainty. Hurricane Isaias, which struck the Florida Panhandle on October 9, falls in the fourth quarter, though several modelers and Gallagher Re describe it as a manageable event, and Gallagher Re reported on October 21 that global insured catastrophe losses for the first nine months of 2026 were the lowest since 2019.

What happens next is a matter of timing. The full third-quarter report on November 12 will give the combined ratio, the segment breakdown and the large-loss figures that the preliminary release omits. The January 1, 2027 renewals will then show how much of the price decline continues. Hannover Re's subsidiary E+S Rück said on October 19 that it expects strong demand for quality reinsurance protection but increasing competition in catastrophe and industrial lines, which suggests that the market's largest players expect to hold their discipline while prices fall. Readers should treat the figures above as preliminary and the target as the company's expectation, not a guarantee, since a single large loss in the final quarter could change the picture.
source_name: Reinsurance News (October 23, 2026) and Munich Re half-year report (July 8, 2026)
image_alt: Natural catastrophe imagery representing reinsurance losses and results (illustrative)
key_points: Munich Re reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 net profit of approximately €1.7 billion, above the analyst consensus of €1.479 billion, citing very pleasing operating performance in all segments, below-average major-loss expenditure in property and casualty reinsurance and a strong investment result in reinsurance.
Nine-month net result was preliminarily €5.7 billion, following €2.211 billion in the second quarter and a record €3.925 billion in the first half.
The full-year 2026 net profit target was raised from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion; in August the company had said it was 'firmly on track' for €6.3 billion.

Subject to major-loss developments, Munich Re intends to keep strengthening its balance sheet where appropriate in the fourth quarter, which the report suggests could include reserves; final third-quarter results are due on November 12, 2026.

In the first half the combined ratio in property and casualty reinsurance was 68.9% in the second quarter with major losses at 4.9% of net insurance revenue against an expected 18%, while July renewals saw volume fall 9.1% and risk-adjusted prices fall 5.5%.
why_it_matters: Munich Re is one of the world's largest reinsurers, so its results are a gauge of how profitable it is to insure the insurers. A raised target in the fourth quarter of a year with unusually light catastrophe losses says that the benefit of a quiet loss year is being booked, not paid out in claims. The same results also show the other side of the cycle: the company is writing less business at lower prices, and says it is strengthening its balance sheet rather than assuming losses will stay this low. For primary insurers and their customers, strong reinsurer profits help explain why property reinsurance has become cheaper.

title: Selective Insurance's Third Quarter: Operating EPS Up to $2.37 and a 96.8% Combined Ratio as Premiums Fall 7% on Deliberate Pruning
summary: Selective Insurance Group reported third-quarter 2026 non-GAAP operating income of $2.37 per share against $1.75, a GAAP combined ratio of 96.8% against 98.6%, and net premiums written down 7% to $1,122.8 million, while raising its dividend 12% and narrowing 2026 guidance.
description:
Selective Insurance Group's third-quarter results show an insurer that is earning more while selling less. In a press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on October 22, 2026, and discussed on a conference call the next morning, the New Jersey-based company reported net income of $2.11 per diluted share, compared with $1.85 a year earlier, and non-GAAP operating income of $2.37 per diluted share, compared with $1.75. Return on equity was 15.1% and operating return on equity was 16.9%. Chief executive John J. Marchioni said: "We remain focused on maintaining underwriting and pricing rigor in a competitive marketplace."

The underwriting result improved. The GAAP combined ratio was 96.8%, compared with 98.6% in the third quarter of 2025. A combined ratio below 100% means premiums exceeded claims and expenses, so Selective earned an underwriting profit of roughly three cents on each dollar of premium. That happened despite higher catastrophe losses, which added 5.4 points to the ratio. The press release also reports no prior-year casualty reserve development at the segment or line-of-business level, meaning the company neither released nor added to reserves for older casualty claims in the quarter. That detail matters because casualty reserves have been a source of concern for the industry. According to a machine-assisted transcript of the call, management said casualty reserves in the underlying general liability line have been stable for seven straight quarters.

Premium volume moved the other way. Net premiums written, the premium an insurer keeps after paying for reinsurance, were $1,122.8 million, down 7%. Standard Commercial Lines, the largest segment, wrote $867.5 million, down 8%. Standard Personal Lines wrote $96.0 million, also down 8%, and Excess and Surplus Lines wrote $159.3 million, down 2%. The transcript indicates that the decline reflects a deliberate pullback from weaker business, and that retention in the best-performing commercial customer groups was 90%, while retention in the lowest-performing groups, about 10% of premium, fell to 52% from 79%. Because the transcript contains garbled passages, particularly in the question-and-answer section, those call details should be checked against the company's own materials.

Price increases are what offset the volume decline in profit. The average renewal pure price increase, which measures the change in price on renewing policies excluding changes in exposure, was 5.6% in the quarter. Standard Commercial Lines rose 5.7%, Standard Personal Lines 8.1% and Excess and Surplus Lines 1.5%. According to the call transcript, commercial renewal pure price was 6.4% excluding workers' compensation, commercial auto liability pricing rose 11.6%, and personal lines pricing rose 9.3% year to date. Management said commercial auto and general liability "are not yet at our target level of profitability," and that it will keep pushing rate and tightening risk selection.

Investment income is now a major source of earnings. After-tax net investment income was $127.3 million, up 16%. Book value per common share was $55.02, down 5% from the prior quarter because higher interest rates reduce the market value of bonds held, while adjusted book value per share, which strips out that effect, was $62.00, up 2%. In the quarter the company bought back $55 million of shares and the board approved a new $200 million repurchase authorisation. The quarterly dividend was raised 12% to $0.48 per share, payable on December 1, 2026 to holders of record on November 16, 2026.

The company's guidance gives a sense of what it expects for the rest of the year. For 2026 it expects a GAAP combined ratio of 96.5% to 97.5%, including 5.5 points of net catastrophe losses, and the transcript says management expects to land closer to the middle of that range. After-tax net investment income guidance was raised to $490 million from $480 million. The guidance assumes an effective tax rate of 21.5% and weighted average diluted shares of 59.9 million.

Catastrophe losses are a live issue, since Hurricane Isaias struck the Florida Panhandle on October 9, after the quarter ended. The transcript says management expects its Isaias losses to be immaterial. That is consistent with the view of AM Best, which expects the storm to be an earnings event for the industry that should not significantly deplete surplus.

What the results do not show is where growth will come from. With written premium falling 7%, the company is relying on higher prices on the business it keeps and on investment income to grow earnings. If competition intensifies, as other insurers and reinsurers have said it is doing, particularly in commercial property, then pricing power could erode before volumes recover. The Marsh global insurance index recorded a ninth straight quarterly decline in the third quarter, and Selective's own excess and surplus lines pricing, at 1.5%, is far below its 11.6% increase in commercial auto liability, which shows how uneven the market has become.

Readers who want exact figures should use the company's filed press release, which is the source of the numbers above, and treat the call-transcript details as indicative until confirmed.
source_name: Selective Insurance Group Form 8-K press release (October 22, 2026) and Q3 earnings call (October 23, 2026)
image_alt: Commercial and residential buildings representing property and casualty insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Selective reported net income of $2.11 per diluted share against $1.85, and non-GAAP operating income of $2.37 per share against $1.75, with return on equity of 15.1% and operating return on equity of 16.9%.

The GAAP combined ratio improved to 96.8% from 98.6% despite catastrophe losses of 5.4 points, and the company recorded no prior-year casualty reserve development at the segment or line-of-business level.

Net premiums written fell 7% to $1,122.8 million: Standard Commercial Lines $867.5 million (down 8%), Standard Personal Lines $96.0 million (down 8%) and Excess and Surplus Lines $159.3 million (down 2%).
Average renewal pure price rose 5.6%, with Standard Commercial at 5.7%, Standard Personal at 8.1% and Excess and Surplus at 1.5%; after-tax net investment income rose 16% to $127.3 million.

The board raised the quarterly dividend 12% to $0.48 per share and authorised a new $200 million repurchase program; 2026 combined ratio guidance is 96.5% to 97.5% including 5.5 points of catastrophe losses, and after-tax investment income guidance was raised to $490 million from $480 million.
why_it_matters: Selective is a mid-sized US commercial and personal lines insurer, so its results show how the middle of the market is balancing price, volume and profit. The quarter illustrates a trade-off many insurers now face: raise prices and drop weaker accounts to protect margin, and accept lower premium as a result. Falling written premium with a better combined ratio is a sign of discipline, not of weakness, but it also means growth has to come from price and investment income. For customers, it reflects continuing rate increases in commercial auto liability and personal lines.

title: Moody's Holds France at Aa3 With a Negative Outlook, a Reprieve Conditioned on a 2027 Budget, After 10-Year Yields Hit 5.1%
summary: On October 23, 2026 Moody's kept France's sovereign rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook, against widespread expectations of a downgrade to A1, saying the rating assumes a 2027 budget that reduces the deficit and slightly easing social tensions, with the ten-year yield having passed 5.1% for the first time since 2002.
description:
France avoided a credit downgrade on Friday evening, but on terms that leave the government with little room for error. Moody's announced on October 23, 2026 that it was keeping France's sovereign rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook, according to Euronews, Il Sole 24 Ore and MarketScreener. The decision went against the expectations of most economists. ABC Bourse reported on October 21 that a majority of economists expected a one-notch cut from Aa3 to A1, and Il Sole 24 Ore described the outcome as a surprise. Moody's stated that the decision was not a credit action, and the reports note that it offered no signal on whether a rating action is likely soon.

The agency's reasoning is conditional. Moody's said the Aa3 rating assumes that a 2027 budget that reduces the public deficit will be adopted, and that social tensions will ease slightly over the coming months. MarketScreener reported that Moody's cited France's diversified economy and strong public institutions, but warned that political instability could hamper efforts to address fiscal pressures. It also said that "a significant and sustained fiscal effort will still be needed beyond the presidential elections" in April and May 2027, and projected that debt will exceed 120% of GDP in 2027. For context, Moody's cut France from Aa2 to Aa3 in late 2024. Fitch and S&P cut France to A+ in 2025, one notch below Moody's, so Moody's remains the only one of the three to keep France in the Aa category. Selectra reported that Moody's last confirmed the Aa3 negative position on April 10, 2026, while S&P's A+ stable rating dates from May 29 and Fitch's from August 28, and that S&P's next scheduled review is November 27, 2026.

The market backdrop explains why a downgrade was expected. ABC Bourse reported that the French ten-year yield reached 5% on October 21 for the first time since 2002, and Euronews put the move above 5.1% on Wednesday, against about 3.2% before the US-Iran war. Germany's ten-year yield is near 3.4% and the United States' is near 5%, so the gap with Germany, reported at about 170 basis points by MarketScreener and at its highest since 2011 by ABC Bourse, reflects France-specific risk. The fiscal numbers are weak: the deficit was 5.1% of GDP in 2025 and is expected to reach 5.4% in 2026, above the European Union's 3% limit, with the government targeting 5% for 2027. Public debt could reach 121.7% of GDP. The economy contracted by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and stagnated in the second, and growth of only 0.1% is expected in the third. The International Monetary Fund forecasts growth of 0.4% for France this year against 1.1% for the eurozone, and MarketScreener notes that nearly 55% of French debt is held overseas.

The political situation sits behind all of this. Budget talks in the National Assembly are delayed, and adoption before late December is uncertain, according to ABC Bourse. Euronews noted that the social security deficit has widened by more than €5 billion since the review of the relevant bill began, according to minister David Amiel. Protests continued, with a further round on Saturday, October 24 that analysts see as a test for the government. Euronews also reported that retailers and luxury groups suffered from the unrest of October 17: Carrefour shares fell more than 13% after it estimated the cost of the looting at €80 million to €200 million, Kering fell 16% and Hermès 7%. Insurers expect their own bill for that weekend of up to €1.2 billion, according to Morningstar DBRS, whose sovereign analyst Mehdi Fadli said the direct fiscal costs of the protests are likely manageable but that prolonged social tension could constrain policymaking and complicate a 2027 budget.

The government welcomed the outcome. Economy Minister Roland Lescure called it recognition of the strength of the economy and "a call for responsibility," and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the decision contradicted predictions of decline from "those who speculate on French debt," citing a release of diesel stocks expected to lower pump prices from November 1. The analysts cited by Euronews were more cautious. Théophile Legrand of Natixis, who had considered a downgrade the central scenario but largely priced in, read the outlook as Moody's giving France more time with the downgrade risk intact, and called the political uncertainty the most worrying signal. Jérémie Peloso of BCA Research blamed political deadlock and a lack of budget ambition and called French debt a "time bomb," while flagging that bond buyers could return on dips. Jérôme Mathis of Paris-Dauphine called the spread with Germany the clearest sign of a loss of budgetary and political credibility.

The risks that remain are listed in the coverage: protests, a presidential election in under six months, inflation, weak growth and expected European Central Bank rate increases. Euronews notes that one candidate's proposal to cancel or convert debt held by the European Central Bank is a concern for investors. Selectra points out that there is no automatic link between the rating and a loan rate, because banks also rely on customer deposits and add their own margin, and that fixed-rate loans already signed keep their rate.

What to watch is the budget. If a 2027 budget that cuts the deficit towards 5% passes, Moody's condition is met and the pressure on the outlook eases; if it fails, a downgrade becomes the likely next step. The next dated checkpoint is S&P's review on November 27, 2026. The reports do not discuss the direct effect on French insurers, which hold substantial government debt, so that connection is a matter for insurers' own disclosures and their regulators.
source_name: Euronews (October 24, 2026), Il Sole 24 Ore, MarketScreener, ABC Bourse (October 21, 2026) and Selectra (October 14, 2026)
image_alt: French city skyline representing sovereign credit and public finances (illustrative)
key_points: Moody's affirmed France at Aa3 with a negative outlook on Friday, October 23, 2026, despite a majority of economists expecting a one-notch downgrade to A1; the agency said the decision was not a credit action.

Moody's said the rating assumes a 2027 budget that reduces the deficit is adopted and that social tensions ease slightly, and it expects debt to exceed 120% of GDP in 2027 and a 'significant and sustained fiscal effort' beyond the April-May 2027 presidential elections.

The French ten-year yield rose above 5.1% on Wednesday, October 21, its highest since 2002, against about 3.2% before the US-Iran war; the spread over German Bunds was reported at about 170 basis points, the widest since 2011.

The deficit was 5.1% of GDP in 2025 and is expected to reach about 5.4% in 2026, with the government targeting 5% for 2027; Fitch and S&P already rate France A+, one notch below Moody's, and S&P's next review is November 27.
Analysts quoted by Euronews called the decision a 'brief respite' and not a 'vote of confidence', pointing to political deadlock, continuing protests and a presidential election in under six months.
why_it_matters: A sovereign rating influences what a government pays to borrow, and the cost of government borrowing feeds into mortgage rates, bank funding and the value of the bonds that French insurers and pension funds hold. A downgrade would have put Moody's in line with Fitch and S&P, which already rate France A+. The reprieve gives the government time, but the agency has tied it to passing a budget, so the decisive moment is now the parliamentary vote, not the rating. For businesses that insure French property, the same social tensions that worry Moody's were behind the October 17 riots covered by insurers.

title: UAE's New Insurance Licensing Rules: Central Bank Circular 4/2026 Makes the Business Plan Central, Limits Foreign Insurers to Branches and Adds Personal Sanctions
summary: The Central Bank of the UAE's Insurance Company Licensing Regulation (Circular 4/2026), in force from August 14, 2026, replaces the 2009 Insurance Authority rules, treats foreign insurers as branch applicants only, sets 60-business-day application and decision windows and lets the regulator remove senior managers and board members.
description:
The rules for getting an insurance licence in the United Arab Emirates changed on August 14, 2026, and the change is larger than a routine update. According to the law firm Al Tamimi & Company, the Central Bank of the UAE's Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, issued as Circular No. 4/2026, came into force on that date. It replaces Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Resolution No. 2 of 2009, which was the executive regulation under Federal Law No. 6 of 2007. Its legal basis is Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, and it is to be read together with the central bank's regulations on corporate governance, risk management, fitness and propriety, takaful and minimum capital. Mondaq's summary of the wider legal change explains the background: the 2025 law put banking and insurance supervision under one federal framework run by the central bank, and the former Insurance Authority was merged into it.

The regulation applies to insurance companies, branches of foreign insurers and prospective entrants. Pinsent Masons, in an Out-Law article dated September 29, 2026, adds that insurers incorporated in the Dubai International Financial Centre and Abu Dhabi Global Market are treated as foreign insurers for this purpose. It covers the licensing of insurers and foreign branches, the establishment of insurance branches and subsidiaries inside and outside the UAE, classes of insurance business, and registration, annual renewal and commencement of activities. Al Tamimi notes that the main product classes, life and family, health, personal accident, funds accumulation, property and liability, are substantially unchanged, so existing licensees do not need to be reclassified.

The most visible structural change concerns foreign insurers. Under the regulation, a foreign insurer may be licensed only as a branch, and that includes companies established in the financial free zones. Agent-based licensing is no longer provided for. Pinsent Masons stresses that a foreign insurer writing business onshore needs a central bank licence, that authorisation from its home regulator is not sufficient, and that licences granted in the DIFC and ADGM do not extend onshore. Jessa White, a managing senior associate at the firm, said such insurers cannot rely on their existing home regulator's authorisation. Branches must provide a bank guarantee under Article 95 of the Central Bank Law, according to Annex 1 as described by Al Tamimi.

The process has fixed time limits. Al Tamimi sets out four stages. An application counts as formally received only once it is complete. Applicants then have 60 business days to correct deficiencies; if they do not, the application lapses and they cannot reapply for six months. The central bank must decide within 60 business days, and it must notify its decision within 20 business days, giving reasons for any rejection. These timelines give applicants more certainty, but the six-month bar penalises incomplete filings, which is why Al Tamimi advises preparing the documentation carefully before filing. Annex 1 requires material on group structure, ICT and cybersecurity systems, outsourcing arrangements and Emiratisation plans.

The criteria are where Pinsent Masons sees the biggest shift. Marie Chowdhry, a partner in financial regulation at the firm, called it "a commercially significant change since licensing is no longer a purely technical exercise." The regulator will look at the applicant's commercial proposition, including whether it brings products that the UAE market lacks or that are in strong demand, and whether it will increase the share of premium retained in the country. Refusal grounds expressly include the qualifications of founders and shareholders, the fit and proper process, the robustness and viability of the business plan, and the readiness of corporate governance and risk management. Jessa White advised applicants to treat the business plan as the centre of the application and not as a supporting document. The commentary does not say how the market-contribution test will be weighed against other factors, so its practical effect will become clearer from the regulator's decisions.

Supervision after licensing is also tougher. Al Tamimi reports that the central bank may amend, revoke or impose new licence conditions at any time. It may close a UAE branch for false information, breach of approval conditions, non-compliance or 12 months of inactivity. Companies can apply to withdraw a licence in whole or in part. Sanctions are no longer limited to suspending licensed activity: the regulator may withdraw, replace or restrict the powers of senior managers or board members, impose interim management or bar individuals from the UAE insurance sector. The articles do not give fine amounts under this regulation. Separately, Mondaq notes that unlicensed financial activity under the wider law can bring imprisonment, a fine of AED 50,000 to AED 500 million, or both.

The regulation sits alongside a broader clean-up of who may carry on insurance-related business. Mondaq explains that insurance, reinsurance, takaful and retakaful, and professions such as agents, brokers, surveyors and loss adjusters, consultants, actuaries and health third-party administrators need a licence from the central bank or a financial free zone regulator. Non-financial free zones such as DMCC, JAFZA and RAKEZ fall under the federal law, so a central bank authorisation or no-objection is mandatory there. A DMCC circular of July 1, 2024 required insurance-related entities to obtain a no-objection certificate, and the transition period ended on December 31, 2025. Businesses without one are described as being in breach of both free-zone requirements and federal law. Affected firms can obtain central bank licensing or move to the DIFC or ADGM, depending on their activity and customers.

Some points are not covered by the published commentary. Al Tamimi's article refers to the minimum capital regulation but gives no capital figures, and neither it nor Pinsent Masons states a transition period for existing licensees. Al Tamimi does not give the date the circular was issued. Anyone planning an application or relying on the rules should therefore read the text of Circular 4/2026 and the related capital regulation directly, and take advice, since this article summarises law-firm commentary and is not legal advice.
source_name: Al Tamimi & Company (September 2, 2026), Pinsent Masons Out-Law (September 29, 2026) and Mondaq (2026)
image_alt: Dubai skyline representing the UAE insurance and financial services market (illustrative)
key_points: The Central Bank of the UAE's Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, Circular No. 4/2026, took effect on August 14, 2026 and replaces Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 2 of 2009; it rests on Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, which moved insurance supervision into the central bank.

Foreign insurers can now be licensed only as branches, including branches of companies in the financial free zones, and agent-based licensing is no longer provided for; a home-regulator authorisation does not substitute for a CBUAE licence.

Applicants get 60 business days to fix deficiencies or the application lapses with a six-month bar on reapplying, the central bank has 60 business days to decide and must notify its decision within 20 business days with reasons for any rejection.

Refusal grounds expressly include the fit and proper process, the viability of the business plan and readiness of corporate governance and risk management; Pinsent Masons says the regulator will also weigh whether an applicant brings products the market lacks or raises premium retention in the country.

Sanctions are no longer limited to suspending activity: the CBUAE may withdraw, replace or restrict the powers of senior managers or board members, impose interim management or bar individuals from the UAE insurance sector, and may close a branch after 12 months of inactivity.
why_it_matters: Insurers that want to sell in the UAE now face a licensing test that examines what they bring to the market, not just whether their systems and capital are in order. For foreign groups the route is narrower, because a branch is the only structure available and a home licence does not carry over. For insurers already licensed, the regulation puts senior managers and board members personally within reach of the regulator, which raises the stakes on governance. For policyholders the intended benefit is a market with fewer weakly planned entrants, though the published commentary does not give capital figures or a transition timetable, so firms should read the regulation itself.

title: US Life Insurers' AI-Linked Investments Reach $85.2 Billion, Up 24% in Six Months, as Moody's Warns Its Figure Likely Understates the Exposure
summary: Moody's Ratings reports that US life insurers held $85.2 billion of AI-linked investments at the end of June 2026, up 24% from $69 billion at end-2025 and about 1.4% of cash and invested assets, with data-centre and digital-infrastructure financing growing fastest and the below-investment-grade share rising to 6.1%.
description:
US life insurers have been lending steadily into the artificial intelligence build-out, and a new Moody's Ratings analysis puts a number on it. According to Reinsurance News, which reported the analysis on October 23, 2026, life insurers held $85.2 billion of AI-linked investments at the end of the second quarter of 2026. That is about 1.4% of their cash and invested assets and 2.1% of their fixed-income holdings, up from 1.7% at the end of 2025. It is also 24% higher than the $69 billion held at the end of 2025, a rise over six months. Bloomberg's headline on October 22 carried the same $85 billion figure. An aggregator summary of the report says positions are as of June 30, 2026.

The exposure falls into three groups. The first is debt issued by major technology companies, which stood at $32.2 billion, up 21% from the end of 2025 and equal to about 6.6% of those companies' outstanding debt. Reinsurance News names Oracle, with about $10 billion, and Amazon, with $8.5 billion, and says purchases in the first half of 2026 favoured the higher-rated Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms. The second group, and the fastest growing, is digital-infrastructure financing, at $39.5 billion, up 34%. This funds data-centre buildings, electricity infrastructure and the chips that run AI, including graphics processing units and tensor processing units, and includes asset-backed securities, commercial mortgage-backed securities and other financing. The third group is investments linked to semiconductor manufacturers, which the article names but does not size.

The quality of the newer holdings is the detail to watch. Moody's reports that the below-investment-grade share of the digital-infrastructure financing rose from 4.7% at the end of 2025 to 6.1% in the second quarter of 2026. Below-investment-grade debt, often called junk, pays higher interest because the chance of default is higher. A rising share can mean insurers are accepting more risk in exchange for yield, although the Reinsurance News article does not draw that conclusion; one aggregator summary does, as its own interpretation and not as a Moody's finding.

Moody's is open about the limits of its numbers. It says the total is hard to quantify because of the structures involved: special purpose vehicles, joint ventures, alternative investment funds, commercial mortgage loans and collateralised loan obligations can all channel money into the sector without being labelled as AI investments. As a result, its figures likely underestimate the true exposure. It also points to indirect links, such as guarantees, leases and credit support, through which an insurer can be exposed to a technology company without owning its debt directly. The aggregator summary adds that suppliers of cooling, power and networking equipment, and data-centre real estate, could see credit deterioration if spending slows.

The commitments behind the borrowing are large. Reinsurance News reports that the disclosed future commitments of five major technology companies, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Oracle, are about $2.8 trillion, including leases not yet commenced, purchase agreements and guarantees, compared with $1.2 trillion in 2025, an increase of around 130%. The article also names CoreWeave, OpenAI, Anthropic, NVIDIA, Broadcom and AMD among other participants in the AI sector, and says investment in the global AI ecosystem could total at least $3 trillion over five years, with broader estimates of $3 trillion to $7 trillion. Moody's expects life insurers to remain an important source of funding for the investment-grade debt used to finance these projects.

Moody's lists the risks. Concentration matters because some insurers hold much larger positions than others. Counterparty risks are interconnected, because trouble in one transaction could affect others; examples given include special purpose vehicles that lease equipment to technology companies and chipmakers that finance their own customers. Physical and regulatory constraints, such as limits on electricity supply, permitting requirements and local opposition to data centres, could delay construction, raise financing costs and reduce the cash flow available to repay debt, and the article cites 2026 regulatory developments in New Jersey and Texas. Funding gaps may force companies to raise more debt where planned capital spending exceeds operating cash flow.

On the question of scale, Moody's conclusion is measured: at current levels, AI-related investments remain a relatively modest component of insurers' overall assets. Looking ahead, Reinsurance News reports that it expects AI-related holdings to increase by $50 billion to $100 billion by the end of 2027, if global digital infrastructure spending reaches $1 trillion that year. That would put the exposure at roughly $135 billion to $185 billion on the starting figure, a calculation from the published numbers and not a Moody's forecast of the total.

This analysis concerns insurers' investments, which is a different question from their use of AI in business. A separate Moody's survey of 58 insurers, brokers and reinsurers, reported by Insurance Business on October 18, found that about two-thirds have deployed AI broadly or in several production use cases, and that Moody's expects a neutral-to-positive credit effect from it. The investment-side findings above are about the risk on the balance sheet. Readers who want precise figures should consult the Moody's report itself, since the numbers here come from press summaries of it.
source_name: Reinsurance News (October 23, 2026), Bloomberg (October 22, 2026) and Insurance Business (October 18, 2026), reporting Moody's Ratings analyses
image_alt: Data centre server racks representing AI infrastructure financing (illustrative)
key_points: Moody's Ratings estimates US life insurers' AI-linked investments at $85.2 billion at end-June 2026, about 1.4% of cash and invested assets and up 24% from $69 billion at end-2025; the share of fixed income rose to 2.1% from 1.7%.

Debt of major technology companies was $32.2 billion, up 21%, about 6.6% of those companies' outstanding debt, including roughly $10 billion of Oracle and $8.5 billion of Amazon; digital-infrastructure financing was $39.5 billion, up 34%.
The below-investment-grade share of digital-infrastructure financing rose from 4.7% at end-2025 to 6.1% in the second quarter of 2026.

Moody's says its figures likely understate total exposure because structures such as special purpose vehicles, joint ventures, alternative funds and CLOs make aggregation difficult, and indirect links via guarantees and leases are not fully captured; the five largest tech groups' disclosed future commitments are about $2.8 trillion against $1.2 trillion in 2025.

Moody's concludes the investments remain a relatively modest part of insurers' assets, but projects an increase of $50 billion to $100 billion by end-2027 if global digital infrastructure spending reaches $1 trillion that year.
why_it_matters: Life insurers invest premiums for decades to pay future claims and annuities, so where they put that money affects the security of policyholders. AI-related debt is a small share of assets today, which is why Moody's calls it modest, but it is growing quickly and the riskier part is growing faster than the safer part. The practical risk is concentration and hidden links: an insurer may hold debt of one technology company, data-centre bonds backed by another and structured products tied to a third, all exposed to the same slowdown. Policyholders do not need to act, but regulators and rating agencies will be watching which insurers hold the largest positions.
